mcqs.q: Composite resin is best described as:
opts: The most popular tooth-coloured restorative material, retained by micromechanical adhesion
mcqs.explain: Composites are the most popular tooth-coloured material (replacing silicate/acrylic) and are retained primarily by micromechanical adhesion.

mcqs.q: Composite is retained in the tooth mainly by:
mcqs.explain: Composites bond micromechanically to enamel and dentin, so mechanical retention features are usually not required.

mcqs.q: Composites are indicated for restorations of:
mcqs.explain: Composites are used for Class I–V restorations, foundations/core build-ups, sealants, esthetic procedures, splinting and indirect inlays/onlays.

mcqs.q: Which is an ESTHETIC indication for composite?
mcqs.explain: Esthetic uses include full veneers and diastema (gap) closures.

mcqs.q: Closing a midline gap with composite is termed:
mcqs.explain: Diastema closure restores a space between teeth using composite (an esthetic enhancement procedure).

mcqs.q: The PRIMARY contraindication to composite relates to:
opts: Inability to isolate the field from oral fluids
mcqs.explain: Composite must be bonded in a fluid-free field; if the site cannot be isolated from saliva/oral fluids, composite should not be used.

mcqs.q: For composite restorations, the use of a rubber dam is:
mcqs.explain: Rubber dam isolation is mandatory for composite procedures; if total isolation is impossible, amalgam may be the material of choice.

mcqs.q: If a site cannot be isolated, the material of choice becomes:
mcqs.explain: When the field cannot be protected from contamination, amalgam (which does not require bonding) is preferred.

mcqs.q: For a patient with heavy occlusion or bruxism where the restoration bears all the load:
opts: Amalgam is usually preferred (composite has less wear resistance)
mcqs.explain: With heavy occlusion/bruxism or all occlusal contacts on the restoration, amalgam is usually preferred because composite has lower wear resistance.

mcqs.q: A composite restoration extending onto the ROOT surface may show:
opts: Gap formation from polymerization shrinkage (poor marginal integrity)
mcqs.explain: On the root surface, polymerization shrinkage can cause gap formation/microleakage at the composite-root junction.

mcqs.q: To reduce microleakage of a composite on the root surface, you can place beneath it a:
mcqs.explain: A resin-modified glass-ionomer liner under the composite on the root reduces microleakage, gap formation and recurrent caries (sandwich technique).

mcqs.q: Bonding of composite to enamel relies on:
opts: Acid-etch microporosities filled by resin, forming resin tags
mcqs.explain: Acid-etching creates microporosities in enamel that the resin flows into, forming resin tags — micromechanical bonding.

mcqs.q: The MOST common advantage of composite is:
mcqs.explain: Esthetics is the most commonly cited advantage of composite restorations.

mcqs.q: Composite is considered CONSERVATIVE because:
opts: Less tooth extension is needed and mechanical retention is usually unnecessary
mcqs.explain: Bonded composite needs less extension, no uniform depth and usually no mechanical retention — conserving tooth structure.

mcqs.q: An advantage of composite over amalgam regarding temperature is its:
mcqs.explain: Composite has low thermal conductivity, reducing thermal sensitivity (amalgam conducts heat/cold more).

mcqs.q: A key advantage of bonded composite for the remaining tooth is:
opts: Increased strength of the remaining tooth structure
mcqs.explain: Bonding to tooth structure gives good retention, less microleakage, minimal interfacial staining and increased strength of the remaining tooth.

mcqs.q: The PRIMARY disadvantage of composite restorations is:
mcqs.explain: Polymerization shrinkage is the primary disadvantage, predisposing to gap formation and microleakage.

mcqs.q: Composite is also valued because it is:
mcqs.explain: Composite restorations can be repaired (rather than fully replaced) — a clinical advantage.

mcqs.q: Which restoration would composite be LEAST suitable for?
opts: A heavily loaded occlusal restoration in a bruxist
mcqs.explain: Composite is least suitable where it bears all the heavy occlusal load (bruxism), due to lower wear resistance — amalgam is preferred.

mcqs.q: Composite can be used for 'preventive resin restorations', which are:
opts: Conservative composite restorations combined with sealants
mcqs.explain: Sealants and preventive resin restorations are conservative composite restorations preserving sound tooth structure.

mcqs.q: Composite has historically replaced which older tooth-coloured materials?
mcqs.explain: Composites have completely replaced silicate cement and acrylic resin as the popular tooth-coloured materials.

mcqs.q: Composite can also be used (indirectly) as:
mcqs.explain: Indirect composite inlays and onlays are a recognised indication for composite material.

saqs.q: List the indications for composite restorations.
saqs.a: Class I–V restorations, core build-ups, sealants/preventive resin restorations, esthetic procedures (veneers, diastema closure), splinting, non-carious lesions, inlays/onlays.
Poor isolation (cannot keep fluid-free), heavy occlusion/bruxism, and root-surface extension (shrinkage/gap).

saqs.q: Why is rubber dam mandatory for composite, and what is the alternative if isolation fails?
saqs.a: Composite must bond in a fluid-free field; if isolation cannot be achieved, use amalgam instead.

saqs.q: How does composite bond to enamel?
saqs.a: By micromechanical adhesion: acid-etch creates microporosities filled by resin forming resin tags.
Esthetics, conservative, bonded (strengthens tooth, less microleakage), low thermal conductivity, repairable.
Polymerization shrinkage (gaps/microleakage), technique-sensitive, lower wear resistance, more time-consuming.

saqs.q: How is microleakage of a root-surface composite reduced?
saqs.a: By placing a resin-modified glass-ionomer liner beneath it (sandwich technique).
